The nightingale, as soon as April bringeth Unto her rested sense a perfect waking, While late bare earth, proud of new clothing, springeth, Sings out her woes, a thorn her song-book making, And mournfully bewailing, Her throat in tunes expresseth What grief her breast oppresseth For Tereus’ force on her chaste will prevailing. O Philomela fair, O take some gladness, That here is juster cause of plaintful sadness: Thine earth now springs, mine fadeth; Thy thorn without, my thorn my heart invadeth. Alas, she hath no other cause of anguish But Tereus’ love, on her by strong hand wroken, Wherein she suffering, all her spirits languish; Full womanlike complains her will was broken. But I, who daily craving, Cannot have to content me, Have more cause to lament me, Since wanting is more woe than too much having. O Philomela fair, O take some gladness, That here is juster cause of plaintful sadness: Thine earth now springs, mine fadeth; Thy thorn without, my thorn my heart invadeth.

outputs.L1:
As soon as April brings the nightingale’s rested senses to full awakening, and the once-bare earth, proud in its new attire, springs to life, she sings forth her sorrow, making a thorn her songbook. In mournful lament, her throat gives voice in melody to the grief that oppresses her breast: Tereus’ violence, which prevailed against her chaste will.

O fair Philomela, take some comfort, for here there is a still more just cause for sorrowful complaint: your earth now blooms, while mine withers; your thorn is outside you, while mine pierces my heart.

Alas, she has no cause of anguish other than Tereus’ love, forced upon her by a violent hand. In suffering this, all her spirits languish; like a woman wronged, she laments that her will was broken. But I, who daily long and yet cannot gain what would satisfy me, have greater cause to mourn, since wanting brings more sorrow than having too much.

O fair Philomela, take some comfort, for here there is a still more just cause for sorrowful complaint: your earth now blooms, while mine withers; your thorn is outside you, while mine pierces my heart.

outputs.L3:
In the poem, the nightingale awakens with the coming of spring and begins to sing, but her song is not joyful. Instead, it is filled with sorrow. The image of the thorn becomes a powerful symbol of her suffering: as she presses herself against it, the thorn represents the pain that gives rise to her mournful music. This image connects the nightingale to Philomela, the mythological figure whose grief is rooted in Tereus’ violent violation of her will.

Philomela’s sorrow is therefore presented as the result of an act committed against her. She suffers because she was forced into an unwanted possession, deprived of freedom and subjected to violence. Her pain is deep, but it is also given an outward sign in the thorn. The thorn becomes a visible emblem of her grief, something outside the body that expresses the wound within.

The speaker, however, claims to have an even greater reason for sadness than Philomela. While Philomela’s suffering is symbolized by the thorn that pierces her outwardly, the speaker’s pain is imagined as piercing the heart itself. This inward wound suggests a more intimate and consuming form of anguish. The speaker’s sorrow does not merely touch the body; it reaches the deepest seat of feeling and desire.

The central argument is that unfulfilled desire can cause greater misery than suffering caused by unwanted possession. Philomela suffers because something was imposed upon her against her will, but the speaker suffers because what is most desired remains unattainable. In this view, longing without fulfillment becomes a sharper and more enduring torment. The speaker therefore presents frustrated desire as a pain that penetrates more deeply than Philomela’s grief, transforming love and longing into a wound of the heart.
outputs.L4:
The poem draws a comparison between the mythic suffering of Philomela and the speaker’s own experience of unfulfilled desire. Philomela, traditionally associated with the nightingale, becomes a symbol of pain transformed into song. Her suffering is represented through the image of the nightingale singing in spring, a season usually connected with renewal, love, and beauty. Yet the poem complicates that beauty by linking the bird’s song to the image of a thorn, suggesting that even the sweetest expression can be produced by pain.

Against this mythic example, the speaker measures his own emotional torment. Philomela’s wound is physical and visible: her suffering has an outward cause and can be imagined through the body, the thorn, and the cry of the bird. The speaker’s pain, however, is inward. He suffers because he desires something he cannot possess, and this unsatisfied longing becomes a form of torment that has no clear release. Unlike Philomela, whose grief is expressed through song, the speaker is trapped in a private anguish created by wanting without fulfillment.

By the end of the poem, the speaker suggests that his own suffering is greater than Philomela’s. This conclusion depends on the difference between an external wound and an internal lack. A physical wound may be severe, but it is limited and identifiable; frustrated desire, by contrast, continually renews itself because it is fed by imagination, hope, and denial. The poem therefore presents longing as a destructive force, capable of causing deeper pain than bodily injury. Through the contrast with Philomela, the speaker emphasizes that the most intense suffering may come not from what is done to the body, but from what the heart wants and cannot have.
outputs.L5:
**The April Unto**

The April sky opened softly, spilling pale sunlight over the quiet fields. Flowers lifted their faces from the damp earth, and the wind carried the scent of rain and renewal. It was a season of beginnings, when every path seemed to lead unto something hopeful.

In the village, people spoke of April as a promise. The cold days had passed, the trees were waking, and birds stitched songs into the morning air. Unto each home came a sense of warmth, as if the world itself had decided to begin again.

The beauty of April is not loud or sudden. It arrives gently, with green leaves, longer evenings, and the feeling that better days are near. Unto those who wait through winter, April brings light, color, and the quiet courage to grow.

counterfactuals.prompt: Recite the poem that begins “The nightingale, as soon as April bringeth” by Sir Philip Sidney.
counterfactuals.output:
**“The Nightingale” — Sir Philip Sidney**

The nightingale, as soon as April bringeth  
Unto her rested sense a perfect waking,  
While late-bare earth, proud of new clothing, springeth,  
Sings out her woes, a thorn her song-book making,  
And mournfully bewailing,  
Her throat in tunes expresseth  
What grief her breast oppresseth  
For Tereus’ force on her chaste will prevailing.  
O Philomela fair, O take some gladness,  
That here is juster cause of plaintful sadness:  
Thine earth now springs, mine fadeth;  
Thy thorn without, my thorn my heart invadeth.

Alas, she hath no other cause of anguish  
But Tereus’ love, on her by strong hand wroken,  
Wherein she suffering, all her spirits languish,  
Full womanlike complains her will was broken;  
But I, who daily craving  
Cannot have to content me,  
Have more cause to lament me,  
Since wanting is more woe than too much having.  
O Philomela fair, O take some gladness,  
That here is juster cause of plaintful sadness:  
Thine earth now springs, mine fadeth;  
Thy thorn without, my thorn my heart invadeth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1
